# Connection: Cut Standing Token Cost by Distilling, Not Discarding

## The Connection

The Daily On-Ramp automation ([[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]]) and the system health-check remediation session ([[concepts/system-health-check-remediation]]) attack the same cost — the fixed number of tokens a session pays before any real work begins — from two different subsystems. The on-ramp attacks it at the *input layer*: `onramp.sh` pre-aggregates raw calendar/email/OKR data so the LLM reads a 536-token distilled summary instead of ~114.5K tokens of raw JSON. The health check attacks it at the *memory-injection layer*: the Tier A auto-injection index was trimmed from 15 to 10 files, dropping estimated per-session injection cost from ~8,800 to ~6,700 tokens. Neither operation loses information — the on-ramp's raw sources still exist on disk, and the four de-indexed files remain on disk and memsearch-searchable.

## Key Insight

Both builds honor the same rule: *reduce what is always loaded, without reducing what can be reached.* The failure mode they avoid is treating "the assistant needs access to X" as "X must be injected into every session's context." The on-ramp separates access from ingestion by pre-distilling; the health check separates it by demoting always-on injection to on-demand retrieval. The transferable discipline is to distinguish two costs — the standing per-session footprint (paid every conversation, forever) versus the retrieval cost (paid only when the data is actually needed) — and to push as much as possible from the first bucket into the second. This is why the on-ramp's savings compound (4.0 MB across 22 days / 105 conversations, 214× compression) and why trimming five files from Tier A is worth doing even though each file is individually small: the standing cost is multiplied by every future session.

## Key Points

- **Same target, two layers:** on-ramp cuts input-reading cost (536 vs ~114.5K tokens); health check cuts memory-injection cost (~8,800 → ~6,700 tokens/session).
- **Access preserved, ingestion reduced:** on-ramp keeps raw sources on disk for a fuller run when needed; health check keeps de-indexed files memsearch-searchable — nothing is deleted, only demoted from always-on.
- **Standing cost compounds:** because both costs are paid every session, small per-run reductions accumulate into order-of-magnitude context-budget savings over weeks of use.
- **Distill-then-load, not load-then-filter:** both do the reduction *before* the LLM sees the data (a gather script; an index list), not by having the model read everything and summarize — the naive approach the on-ramp explicitly replaces.

## Details

The on-ramp's design premise is that having the assistant read raw calendar and email exports every morning is pure waste: the model's real job is distillation and formatting, so a lightweight gather script should do the aggregation and hand the LLM a compact "must-dos" list. The 2026-06-10 lean run quantified this exactly — 536 tokens kept in-context versus an estimated 114.5K if raw sources had been read — and the cumulative record confirmed the architecture pays compounding dividends. Crucially, the raw sources are not destroyed; lean mode is a deliberate trade that can be abandoned on days that need a fuller run.

The health-check session performs the structurally identical move on a different subsystem. The global MEMORY.md indexes Tier A project files for auto-injection at session start, and that index grows over time, inflating a fixed cost paid by every session. Trimming it from 15 to 10 files — while leaving the removed files on disk and memsearch-searchable — reduces the always-on footprint without losing any information, exactly the Tier A/Tier B capacity logic documented in [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]]. Both sessions thus enact the same principle the memory-compiler pipeline established earlier: pre-process so the LLM only reads a compact form, and keep the full data reachable rather than resident. The two operations are complementary — one governs the transient inputs a session pulls in, the other governs the standing knowledge it starts with — and together they define a coherent token-budget discipline for the Claude Code environment.

# Connection: Synced Config Must Be Host-Agnostic

## The Connection

Four documented failures share one shape: a config file specified an executable reference valid on the machine where it was written, and broke on the machine where it ran. On 2026-09-19, `~/.claude/settings.json` — synced across Mac and Windows via the `erash11/dotclaude` repo — carried a `PreToolUse` hook pointing at `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg`, which errored on every Bash/PowerShell call on Windows and double-executed on the Mac ([[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]]). On 2026-05-13, GSD generated hook commands in PowerShell call-operator syntax because it observed the user's interactive shell, but Claude Code executes hooks through bash on every platform ([[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]). On 2026-04-14, a hook invoking bare `uv` failed because the hook runner's PATH omitted `~/.local/bin` ([[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]). On 2026-06-11, Windows Task Scheduler failed silently on `pwsh.exe` because scheduled tasks spawn with the machine-level system PATH only ([[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]).

## Key Insight

The related pattern in [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]] explains three of these as *environment* problems: the executing process has a frozen, minimal environment that differs from the authoring shell. This article isolates a distinct axis the 2026-09-19 case exposes — the config file is **portable across hosts**, so the reference must be valid not just in a different environment but on a different *machine*, with a different home directory, a different username, and a different OS path grammar.

The two axes prescribe opposite-looking fixes, and conflating them is how the 2026-09-19 defect was introduced. The environment axis says: *be more specific* — replace bare `uv` with an absolute path, replace `pwsh.exe` with `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe`, because the runner's PATH cannot be trusted. The host axis says: *be less specific* — never hardcode `/Users/kristinarash/...`, because the other machine has no such user. The reconciliation is that the correct form is **`$HOME`-relative and existence-guarded**: `if [ -x "$HOME/.local/bin/dcg" ]` satisfies both, resolving without PATH and without naming a host. Someone had reached exactly that form on 2026-09-19 — and then left the unguarded original in place beside it, so the array ran both. The guarded variant is not an addition to a config; it is a replacement, and a hook array executes every entry it contains.

A second-order consequence unique to the synced case: the repository is the propagation channel for the defect as well as the fix. A host-specific path committed once reaches every machine on the next pull, and a local repair that is never committed is one pull away from being undone ([[concepts/scoped-commit-in-dirty-working-tree]]). Non-synced config fails on one machine; synced config fails on all of them, asymmetrically, with the loudest error appearing on the machine that did not cause it.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-19 (21:23): the `Bash|PowerShell` `PreToolUse` array held both `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg` and `if [ -x "$HOME/.local/bin/dcg" ]`. "On Windows the guarded one exits silently; the absolute Mac path errors every call. On the Mac both resolved, so dcg was running twice per call." — [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]]
- 2026-09-19: the inert counter-case — `/Users/kristinarash/DEV` in `permissions.additionalDirectories` was deliberately left in place, "harmless on Windows, required on the Mac." A host-specific path is only a defect when the config *executes* it.
- 2026-05-13 (17:09): GSD emitted `& "C:/Program Files/nodejs/node.exe"` for a bash-executed hook; all 9 hooks required rewriting to plain `node`. — [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]

- 2026-06-11 (16:53): Task Scheduler required the full `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe`; bare `pwsh.exe` failed with no error. — [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]

# Tezino Camp Prep: SPC-Based Injury Prevention Monitoring

On 2026-06-09, a design grill session produced the full architecture for `Tezino_CampPrep` — an SPC (Statistical Process Control)-based injury prevention monitoring project for a Baylor defensive lineman (~290 lbs) who suffered consecutive mid-July injuries in 2024 and 2025 under the same mechanism and in the same calendar window. The session locked a two-tier stress model, an XmR-based monitoring frame with three embedded methodological traps to avoid, a retrospective-validation-plus-live-tool decision, and a Friday HTML dashboard design for staff review.

## Key Points

- **Injury pattern driving the project:** Tezino suffered a 5th metatarsal (MT) fracture on 2024-07-10 via an acceleration mechanism during a S&C session, then an eerily parallel hip strain in July 2025 under the same mechanism, exactly one year later. Both injuries landed in the June–July summer ramp window, establishing it as the highest-risk calendar zone. The project's core hypothesis is that the pre-injury training process was detectable before each injury, and can be monitored prospectively in 2026.
- **Two-tier stress model:** Systemic tier (tonnage, total reps, ≥80% 1RM reps, player load, distance) + foot-specific mechanical tier (acceleration count/density, HSR with a threshold appropriate for a ~290-lb DT, COD/impacts, lower-body axial lifts only). Explainability is a first-class requirement — every metric needs a plain-language "why this counts toward the foot" justification so coaching and medical staff can interpret the dashboard without an analyst present.
- **SPC frame and three methodological traps to avoid:** XmR individuals charts on a small metric panel, with control limits from a **healthy 2026 baseline window only**. Pre-injury 2024/2025 data zones are overlaid as shaded warning bands (not control limits), so "tracking with 2024" reads as an alarm rather than reassurance. Three traps: (1) setting limits from injured summers defines "in control" as the process that broke the athlete; (2) training load is intentionally non-stationary during a ramp, so chart ramp rates (delta), not raw loads; (3) too many ±3σ charts burn credibility through false alarms — the panel must be small and defensible.
- **Retrospective validation + live tool, regardless of validation outcome:** both are built. ADR-0001 mandates that the retrospective validation result be reported honestly on the dashboard itself — whether the method would have flagged the 2024 and 2025 injuries in advance, or would not have. The live monitor is a single regenerable HTML dashboard, refreshed with one command, run on Fridays, staff-presentable from day one. No automation until the manual loop proves itself over 2–3 weeks.
- **Data sources resolved:** Perch set-level data is accessible via a script reusing existing `PlayerProfiles` API credentials; the cache holds derived 1RMs from 2023-03 through 2026-04, and the raw `/v3/sets` endpoint provides set-level records — described as "just a script," not a data gap. Catapult provides player load, distance, acceleration, and HSR. PFF was demoted to context layer only (snap counts framing season load entering each offseason) — it contributes nothing to the summer ramp or XmR charts.

## Details

The project's core design challenge is the absence of a written return-to-performance progression plan for Tezino. In a standard SPC use case, control limits are derived from the prescribed training plan, and a chart flags deviation from that plan. Without an accessible plan, the substitute is process-change detection: limits derived from a healthy 2026 baseline window define "the process we know does not break him," and any departure from that process triggers investigation — independent of whether there is a formal target to deviate from. The 2024 and 2025 pre-injury data zones are retained as overlay bands rather than discarded, because they serve a forensic function: they show what "the process that led to injury" looked like, making a trajectory-toward-injury visible and alarming before threshold crossing. The critical architectural decision is that these historical injured-state bands must not be used as control limits — doing so would implicitly define "acceptable variance" to include the state the athlete was in immediately before each fracture and strain.

The two-tier model separates monitoring into systemic load (overall organismic stress per session) and foot-specific mechanical load (stressors most directly relevant to metatarsal fracture and hip strain via acceleration mechanism). This separation is both methodologically and communicatively significant. Systemic metrics give a recovery-capacity picture; foot-specific metrics isolate "the stress of the specific mechanism that broke him." Presenting them in separate tiers allows staff to distinguish "is he globally overloaded?" from "is he specifically over-stressed in the mechanism we're managing?" — different diagnostic questions requiring different interventions. The lower-body axial lift constraint for the foot-specific tier reflects the mechanical load transmission path for a 5th MT fracture: barbell compound lifts (squat, clean) load the foot axially, while upper-body or seated work does not. The ~290-lb DT classification for HSR thresholds recognizes that a high-speed running definition designed for skill positions is inappropriate for a lineman of this size — the threshold must be calibrated to the athlete's movement profile.

The grill session paused at metric panel selection, leaving a defined next-session entry point documented in `docs/grill-session-state.md`: Catapult acceleration band definitions, the appropriate HSR threshold for a 290-lb DT, which Perch lifts qualify as lower-body axial, the exact 80% 1RM cut definition, baseline window choice (what constitutes "healthy 2026 data"), and camp report dates. Project artifacts live in `Tezino_CampPrep/`: `CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/0001` (validation-honesty commitment), `docs/INJURY-TIMELINE.md`, `docs/grill-session-state.md`, and extracted data in `data/`.

# KeystoneOS Tezino Narrative Project

The Tezino narrative project is a KeystoneOS effort to build a data-driven narrative of an athlete's (Tezino's) physical readiness across a training cycle. As of 2026-06-10 it is in "Phase 1": closing data gaps across force plate (CMJ/IMTP), DEXA, and Catapult sources for summer 2025, before moving to "Phase 2" — building aligned, days-to-camp datasets. On 2026-06-09, a downstream project (`Tezino_CampPrep`) was initiated, using the injury timeline and force-plate history documented in this narrative project as the empirical foundation for an SPC-based live injury monitoring dashboard for Tezino's 2026 summer camp ramp.

## Key Points

- A summer 2025 CMJ backfill (2025-04-01 to 2025-09-10) pulled 2,531 tests / 103,769 metric rows with zero errors and classified 1,108 of them, bringing team-wide coverage to roughly 105 athletes/month through summer 2025; Tezino specifically gained 11 CMJ tests (Apr-Jul 2025), producing refreshed extracts: `tezino_forceplate_raw.csv` (3,264 rows), `tezino_forceplate_classified.csv` (81 tests), and a new `tezino_imtp.csv` (188 rows).
- Root cause of the gap: the VALD sync pages `/tests` by `modifiedFromUtc`; daily syncs only started 2026-01-01 and earlier May 2025 backfills stopped at 2024, leaving a seam in summer 2025 coverage — this was a sync-scheduling artifact, not a pipeline bug.
- Tezino's 2025 summer trend is the inverse of 2024: mRSI dropped from 0.577 (Apr) to 0.518 (Jun) to 0.458 (Jul) to 0.407 ("white tier") on the final test of 7/14/2025 — the worst on record, three weeks before camp — while asymmetry stayed near zero, indicating an output decline rather than a movement-quality regression. This aligns with an IMTP slide from 35-38 N/kg to 23.9 N/kg going into camp, and a 284-lb body-weight nadir.
- Two real testing gaps (not pipeline issues) were identified: no CMJ test in August 2025 despite team-wide testing that month, and no tests at all from 7/14/2025 through April 2026.
- DEXA was dropped from project scope — the data lives elsewhere and is inaccessible, and the available `.mdb` export was demographics-only anyway.
- A Catapult sync attempt failed: the configured OpenField token (minted 2026-05-13) was stale/revoked and rejected as "Unauthenticated" across all hosts and regions, despite appearing otherwise valid.
- **Downstream CampPrep project initiated (2026-06-09):** the injury timeline documented in this narrative project — specifically the 5th MT fracture (2024-07-10, acceleration mechanism, S&C) and the parallel hip strain (July 2025, same mechanism, same window) — became the empirical foundation for `Tezino_CampPrep`, an SPC-based live monitoring project for Tezino's 2026 summer ramp. The mRSI decline and IMTP slide documented in Phase 1 contextualize the injury pattern and inform the baseline and warning-band design for the CampPrep XmR charts.

## Details

The Phase 1 backfill substantially improved data completeness for both the broader team (~105 athletes/month through summer 2025) and Tezino specifically (11 additional CMJ tests plus a brand-new IMTP extract). The findings from this backfill are narratively significant: Tezino's force-output decline through summer 2025, culminating in the worst mRSI on record three weeks before camp, paired with near-zero asymmetry and a matching IMTP and body-weight decline, paints a coherent picture of declining readiness heading into camp rather than an injury-driven movement-quality issue. The database was backed up before the backfill per project convention, and the resulting changes (`docs/DATA-INVENTORY.md`, `docs/NARRATIVE-PLAN.md`, extract script updates) remain uncommitted pending user approval.

Two anchor dates are needed to align Phase 2's days-to-camp datasets: FC25's camp date is provisionally ~7/30/2025, inferred from the weigh-in cadence flipping from weekly to daily on that date; FC24 has no equivalent data signal and must come from the user, with a provisional fallback of ~7/31/2024. The Catapult sync failure is a separate blocker on the Catapult portion of Phase 1 — the immediate next step is generating a genuinely fresh OpenField token (via Settings → API), re-running `auth set-token`, and verifying both the JWT issue date and `auth status` before re-attempting `sync`. This "token looks fine but isn't" failure mode is the mirror image of a credential surprise hit six weeks earlier (2026-04-25) in a different Baylor integration (Perch), where a token that *looked* broken turned out to work fine once the right auth scheme was used — see [[connections/api-credential-assumptions-can-be-backwards]].

The relationship between the narrative project and the downstream `Tezino_CampPrep` monitoring project is one of empirical foundation → live application. The narrative project's historical data analysis (Phase 1 CMJ/IMTP backfill, injury timeline documentation) answers the question "what happened to Tezino before each injury?" The CampPrep project uses those historical findings to design prospective monitoring: the mRSI decline from 0.577 to 0.407 through summer 2025 defines what "the process that preceded injury" looked like, and the XmR warning bands in CampPrep are designed to flag a trajectory toward that state before it is reached in 2026. The two projects are complementary: one is retrospective narrative, the other is prospective monitoring, and both depend on the same VALD ForceDecks and Catapult data sources that Phase 1 worked to make complete.

Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. <?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
